passages.t: Honest scales, and a city built up
passages.happening:
The chapter opens in the marketplace. ‘Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, but an accurate weight is His delight’ (verse 1). Then pride: ‘When pride comes, disgrace follows, but with humility comes wisdom’ (verse 2).

Several sayings make one point from different sides: the upright are guided and rescued by their integrity, and the wicked are caught in their own wickedness. ‘The integrity of the upright guides them, but the perversity of the faithless destroys them’ (verse 3). ‘Riches are worthless in the day of wrath, but righteousness brings deliverance from death’ (verse 4).

Then the view widens to the whole town. ‘When the righteous thrive, the city rejoices’ (verse 10). ‘By the blessing of the upright a city is built up, but by the mouth of the wicked it is torn down’ (verse 11). ‘A gossip reveals a secret, but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence’ (verse 13). ‘For lack of guidance, a nation falls, but with many counselors comes deliverance’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 10 set the pattern. Chapter 11 carries it out of the home and into the public square: trade, lending, neighbors, the city, the nation. The fear of the LORD has to be seen at the scales and in the grain market.

Israel's trade ran on weighed silver long before coins were common. A merchant carried a set of stone weights in a bag and used a hand balance. Many small inscribed stone weights from Judah in the later years of the kings have been found, and they differ slightly from one another, which shows how much room there was for cheating. The law forbade carrying two sets of weights, one heavy for buying and one light for selling, and the prophets attacked merchants who did it. Verse 1 calls dishonest scales an abomination, the same strong word the law uses for idolatry.

A town's elders sat in council at the gate, and kings relied on advisers. So the sayings about counsel and the city were practical. A whole town can rise or fall with the honesty of its people.
passages.later: The law said, ‘You must maintain accurate and honest weights and measures’ (Deuteronomy 25:15), and the prophet Micah asked, ‘Can I excuse dishonest scales or bags of false weights?’ (Micah 6:11).
passages.asks: The chapter puts honesty in business under God's eye. Ask where you might be tempted to use two sets of weights, one for yourself and one for others. And ask whether your words help to build up the place where you live, or tear it down.

passages.t: Kindness, and a ring in the wrong place
passages.happening:
‘He who puts up security for a stranger will surely suffer, but the one who hates indebtedness is secure’ (verse 15). ‘A gracious woman attains honor, but ruthless men gain only wealth’ (verse 16). ‘A kind man benefits himself, but a cruel man brings trouble on himself’ (verse 17).

‘The wicked man earns an empty wage, but he who sows righteousness reaps a true reward’ (verse 18). The perverse in heart are detestable to the LORD, ‘but the blameless in their walk are His delight’ (verse 20).

Then a picture: ‘Like a gold ring in a pig’s snout is a beautiful woman who lacks discretion’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Standing surety meant pledging to cover another person's debt if he failed to pay. A man could lose his land or even his freedom for someone else's failure. The warning is against rash promises that put a family's living at risk, not against generosity, as verses 24 and 25 make plain.

Verse 16 sets a gracious woman beside ruthless men. Honor, the lasting thing, belongs to her. They only get money.

Verse 22 uses two things every first reader knew. Pigs were unclean under Israel's law, and a gold ring in the nose was a woman's jewelry, like the one Abraham's servant gave to Rebekah (Genesis 24:47). The picture is meant to shock: a costly ornament wasted on a snout rooting in the mud. Beauty is not condemned. It is shown to be wasted when it is not joined to good sense. The book holds men to the same standard, as the ruthless men of verse 16 show.

Verses 1 and 20 both use the pair abomination and delight. Much of the chapter sits between those two words, under the LORD's own judgment.
passages.later: Paul, writing about generosity, uses the same picture of sowing as verse 18: ‘Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously’ (2 Corinthians 9:6).
passages.asks: Kindness and cruelty both come back to the one who shows them. Ask which of the two people around you are receiving from you this week. And ask whether you value beauty, in yourself or in others, more than good sense and a gracious heart.

passages.t: The generous refreshed, and a tree of life
passages.happening:
‘One gives freely, yet gains even more; another withholds what is right, only to become poor’ (verse 24). ‘A generous soul will prosper, and he who refreshes others will himself be refreshed’ (verse 25). ‘The people will curse the hoarder of grain, but blessing will crown the one who sells it’ (verse 26).

‘He who trusts in his riches will fall, but the righteous will thrive like foliage’ (verse 28). ‘The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life, and he who wins souls is wise’ (verse 30).

The chapter ends with an argument from lesser to greater: “If the righteous receive their due on earth, how much more the ungodly and the sinner!” (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
Verses 24 to 26 form a tight group on giving and holding back. The surprise is that the giver gains and the hoarder loses.

Verse 26 pictures a grain dealer who keeps back his stock in a lean year, waiting for prices to climb while his neighbors go hungry. That happened wherever grain was the staple food and harvests were uncertain. The town curses him. The one who sells when people need bread is honored.

The tree of life in verse 30 reaches back to Eden. A righteous life gives life to others, the way a fruit tree feeds people around it.

Verse 31 argues from the smaller to the greater. If even the righteous are dealt with in this life, how much more will the wicked be.
passages.later: Paul gives Timothy the same warning as verse 28: tell the rich ‘not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy’ (1 Timothy 6:17). And Peter quotes verse 31 in its Greek form, applying it to believers suffering for Christ's name: “If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?” (1 Peter 4:18).
passages.hard:
What does verse 30 mean by saying that he who wins souls is wise?

The phrase has become familiar as a call to share the faith, but the Hebrew is harder than the English suggests. Literally it says that one who takes lives, or souls, is wise, and elsewhere taking a life usually means killing (1:19).

Interpreters handle this in three main ways. Many read it positively in context: the righteous person, like a tree of life, draws others in and wins them over, gaining their trust and bringing them toward life. Some modern translations follow the ancient Greek translation, which reads the line differently, so that it speaks of violence taking lives away, a contrast with the first line. Others keep the Hebrew and hear a wordplay: the wise capture people as surely as a violent man does, but for life instead of death.

What is clear is that the verse is a saying about the life-giving influence of the righteous, not a technical instruction about evangelism. Christians who apply it to sharing the faith are drawing a fair extension from that theme, as long as they do not build too much on a phrase whose exact sense is uncertain.
passages.asks: The chapter says the generous are refreshed. Ask whom you could refresh this week, with time, money or a kind word. And ask what you are holding back, waiting for a better price, when someone near you needs it now.
